reports.title: Card payments
reports.root_cause: Card payments ran into timeouts for about twelve minutes. The connection pool to the payment provider was used up after one slow answer, and waiting requests failed.
steps: Set a shorter timeout for calls to the payment provider and raise the size of the connection pool.
Add an alert on the share of used connections of the pool.
Compare with the report of 22 October for the same service.

reports.title: Cart
reports.root_cause: Carts with more than 200 lines were larger than a cache entry may be and were not saved. Users saw an empty cart after they reloaded the page.
steps: Split large carts over several cache entries or raise the limit.
Log a warning when a cart comes close to the limit.
Add a test with a cart of 500 lines.

reports.title: Card payments
reports.root_cause: A renewed client certificate was rolled out to one of two instances only. Every second payment request was refused until the other instance was restarted.
steps: Restart both instances after a certificate change and check each of them.
Add the expiry date of the certificate to the monitoring.
Write the roll-out of a certificate down as a checklist.

reports.title: Checkout
reports.root_cause: After a release the address check refused postal codes that hold a space. Orders to such addresses failed at the last step of the checkout.
steps: Roll back the change of the address check or accept postal codes with a space.
Add addresses of every country the shop delivers to as test cases.
Find the orders that failed and tell customer service.

reports.title: Cart
reports.root_cause: Changes to the cart were slow for a few minutes around a deployment. No kind of error stands out in the logs, so the cause could not be pinned down.
steps: Watch the response times during the next deployment.
Check whether the instances were replaced one by one.
Open a new investigation if it happens again.

reports.title: Price calculation
reports.root_cause: The price list of a campaign was loaded twice, and the second load ran into the first. For a short time some prices were answered from the old list.
steps: Let only one load of a price list run at a time.
Publish a new price list only when its load is complete.
Check the orders of that time for wrong prices.

ask.q: Why is the sprint at risk?
ask.a:
The forecast gives 9 % to finish everything that is open (forecast.chance_all_pct). 16 SP in 11 items are not done, and 3 working days are left after today.

Two things weigh most. 7 SP are blocked: KES-1290, which is in its sprint number 4, and KES-1391. And 31 SP were committed, while only 1 of 8 past sprints completed that much.

With 85 % certainty the sprint ends with at least 15 SP done. 13 SP are done now.

ask.q: What are the options, and what does each one buy?
ask.a:
Three moves. For each one the forecast was run again without the items that move.

1. Take out what has not started (3 SP: KES-1390, KES-1400, KES-1408, KES-1422): the chance to finish the rest is 19 %.
2. Take out what is blocked (7 SP: KES-1290, KES-1391): 41 %.
3. Take out both (10 SP): 60 %.

For an even chance 9 SP have to leave the sprint, for 85 % certainty 14 SP. Which items go is for the team and the Product Owner to decide.

ask.q: How far can I trust the forecast?
ask.a:
It is built from 86 working days of this team's own history. Replayed inside past sprints, its 85 % line held in 18 of 18 look-backs. The record of forecasts holds 34 entries; 27 of them belong to closed sprints, and the 85 % line held in all 27.

Two limits. It does not see the 2 open stories without story points (KES-1390, KES-1408). And it assumes that the coming days look like the past ones.

ask.q: What should I raise in the Daily today?
ask.a:
Four points.

1. KES-1290 has been blocked for 6 days and KES-1391 is blocked too. Who can unblock each one, and by when?
2. KES-1360 has been in Review for 18 days. Its pull request is approved and not merged.
3. KES-1373 has been in progress for 13 days, and no pull request names it.
4. 2 pull requests have waited a day or more for a first review. Who takes them today?

The data offers 10 signals that are not in the risk register yet.

I would decide on these first: the sprint does not fit (9 % to finish everything, 9 SP over an even chance), and KES-1290, blocked for 6 days in its sprint number 4.

Then: KES-1391 blocked for 3 days, KES-1360 in Review for 18 days, KES-1373 in progress for 13 days, the 3 items that came in after the start, and the four signs of the pre-mortem.

For each one the register asks the same thing: is it a risk, who owns it, what is done about it, and when do you look again.

This team missed 3 of its 8 closed sprints. Four signs came before a missed sprint more often than before a kept one, and all four show today.

- Load: 119 % of what earlier sprints completed on average. Seen in 3 of 3 missed sprints and in 0 of 4 kept ones.
- Blocked items: 2 open. 3 of 3 missed, 0 of 5 kept.
- Commitment done at this point of the sprint: 42 %. As little or less in 3 of 3 missed, 0 of 5 kept.
- Items added after the start: 21 % of the committed items. 2 of 3 missed, 0 of 5 kept.

This is resemblance, not proof: eight sprints are a short history.

ask.q: Where do our bugs come from?
ask.a:
Three places, going by the facts of the Quality tab.

1. Production. 32 % of the bugs of PI 26.4 were found there, 18 of 56, against 20 % in PI 26.3 (quality.escape_pct). payment-gateway holds 39 % of them.
2. Old behaviour that broke. Regression is the cause behind 38 % of the fixed bugs, and 24 % of the fixed bugs came back after their fix.
3. Work nobody reviewed. Merges without a review move with production bugs a sprint later: r is 0.65 over 18 sprints, and it could be 0.27 to 0.86. A hint, not a proof.

The backlog grows too: 29 bugs are open now, 16 were open at the end of PI 26.3.

I would start with the reviews and the regression tests of payment-gateway. I cannot see who wrote what, and I count nothing per person.

In big batches, and that is where the time goes. Going by the facts of the build server for the last 12 weeks:

1. Half of the changes needed 16.1 days or less from the merge into main to production, 85 % needed 27.2 days (delivery.lead_p50_days). 83 % of that time they waited for a release cut or a hotfix. A build of main that passed took 0.3 hours for half of them.
2. 11 deploys reached production: 3 releases, 7 hotfixes, 1 rollback. 3 of 10 had to be repaired by a rollback or a hotfix (delivery.failed_pct).
3. Size makes the difference. The middle release carried 20 changes, and 4 of 6 releases had to be repaired. The middle hotfix carried 1 change, and 1 of 10 hotfixes had to be repaired.
4. Main was red in 3.3 % of the hours without weekends, against 0.9 % in the 12 weeks before. 9 of 19 failed builds passed when the same build was run again, so look at the tests that fail now and then.

21 changes are merged and not in production yet. Release 4.20.0 is cut and holds all 21.

ask.q: What can I ask you, and what can you see?
ask.a:
I see what this page is built from: the facts of the running sprint, the issues behind each number with their status history, and the forecast with its look-back. I read them through four read-only tools.

I do not see issue titles, comments or people, and I cannot change or send anything.

Ask about the promise, the options, the risks, the bugs, a single issue or the history. In this demo I am a recording: the seven cards are answered, a question of your own is not.
